doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

chapter: San Diego and the state of jazz
title: San Diego's current jazz scene and its Latin influence
summary: Wofford calls the local scene perilous, with major clubs lost but fine players and university programs; Latin music has grown only recently.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: What’s San Diego’s music atmosphere like down here? Can you play here a lot or do you have to travel elsewhere?

Well I think it’s like most cities its size across the country. The jazz scene is perilous at best and from one year to the next it’ll be better than others. Right now it’s not great. We’ve lost a couple of what were the major clubs here. There is always activity and there are wonderful players here, great players working, but I wouldn’t call it a thriving jazz scene right now. But again, I think that’s true in most cities I’ve been in from one year to the next. This next year may be a complete turnaround. But right now it’s not as good as it had been a couple of years ago. But it’s a very vibrant town musically. There’s a lot of interesting stuff going on, a lot of interesting music experimentation and some wonderful, wonderful players and a lot of really wonderful young players. The UCSD Music Department here, the University of California in LaJolla, has a wonderful music department where jazz and experimental music are concerned. And also out at San Diego State University. So they help.
Is there a stronger influence, being that you’re so close to Mexico, in the Latin end of things?

Well it’s interesting. There is now, but that would not have been the case up until even just a few years ago. Typically I would say no, that would not have been the case years © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

ago here. I mean you would draw that conclusion, it seems like an obvious connection, but it’s only been recently that that has really occurred. But now, yeah, it’s very strong. There is more Latin-oriented music of one type of another, whether it’s Brazilian or Afro- Cuban or whatever. And blues are generally active in the city right now than traditional jazz or acoustic jazz. There is, like everywhere, there is a certain amount of contemporary jazz or whatever term you want to use that sometimes is borderline jazz at best, and we have our share of that. Some of it’s fine and some of it’s not so fine, but anyway, if that answers your question.
